title: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
summary: Why one-hot codes fail, how an embedding table is a trainable lookup, how word2vec learns vectors from context with negative sampling, what the geometry means, and how contrastive learning generalizes it.
outcomes: Explain why one-hot codes cannot share knowledge between related items and how an embedding lookup fixes it
Compute one skip-gram negative sampling update by hand and predict which vectors move where
Explain how noise distribution, subsampling and k affect word2vec training
Explain what cosine neighbours and vector analogies do and do not show, including the shifted PMI view
Compute an InfoNCE loss at different temperatures and choose where to take a contrastive representation

lessons.title: From one-hot IDs to a trainable embedding table

blocks.md: In the prerequisite course you trained networks whose inputs were numbers. Words, product IDs, user IDs and other *categorical* inputs are not numbers, so the first question is how to feed them to a network at all. The simplest answer is a **one-hot vector**: give each of the $W$ items in the vocabulary an index, and represent item $i$ as a length-$W$ vector that is all zeros except a 1 at position $i$.

Take a vocabulary of five words: *cat, dog, kitten, car, truck*. One-hot coding gives *cat* = `[1,0,0,0,0]` and *kitten* = `[0,0,1,0,0]`. Every word is exactly as far from every other word. The dot product between any two different one-hot vectors is 0, so their **cosine similarity** (the dot product divided by the two lengths, ranging from -1 to 1) is also 0.

blocks.prompt: A sentiment model has learned from training data that *cat* tends to appear in positive reviews. With one-hot inputs, how much of that knowledge transfers to *kitten*, which never appeared in training?
blocks.reveal: **None.** The weights that multiply the *cat* input position are separate from the weights for the *kitten* position, and nothing ties them together. One-hot coding tells the network that *cat* and *kitten* are as unrelated as *cat* and *truck*. Every word must be learned from its own examples, which fails for rare words. Bengio et al. (2003) proposed learned word vectors to fight this, as part of what they call the curse of dimensionality: test word sequences differ from every sequence seen in training.

blocks.title: Cosine similarity: one-hot codes vs dense vectors

scenes.caption: One-hot codes: each word is similar only to itself. The off-diagonal is all 0, so the representation carries no notion of related words.
Dense 3-dimensional vectors (toy values chosen by hand to mimic trained ones). Now cat and kitten score 0.99 and cat and car score -0.39: similar words sit close together.
The two blocks are the animals and the vehicles. A model that learns something about cat now gets a head start on kitten (0.99) and a little on dog (0.8).

blocks.md: An **embedding** is that dense vector: each item gets a row of $d$ real numbers, with $d$ much smaller than $W$ (often tens to a few hundred). Stacking the rows gives an **embedding matrix** $E$ of shape $W \times d$. Bengio et al. (2003) introduced exactly this for neural language models: a $|V| \times m$ matrix $C$ of free parameters whose row $i$ is the feature vector of word $i$, learned jointly with the rest of the network.

Looking up a row is the same as multiplying the one-hot vector by $E$. The one-hot vector selects one row and zeros out the others, so the network never has to do the full multiplication. Frameworks implement the lookup directly: PyTorch's `nn.Embedding(num_embeddings, embedding_dim)` is documented as "a simple lookup table" whose `weight` has shape `(num_embeddings, embedding_dim)` and is initialized from $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$.

blocks.caption: Multiplying by a one-hot vector selects row 2 (0-based) of the embedding matrix.

blocks.title: An embedding lookup selects rows of E

scenes.caption: The embedding matrix E: 5 words by 3 dimensions, 15 trainable numbers. In a real model they start random and training moves them.
Input token kitten (index 2): the lookup returns row 2, [0.9, 0.0, 0.4]. This is identical to one-hot times E, without the 12 multiplications by zero.
A batch of tokens [cat, car, cat] reads rows 0, 3 and 0. Rows 1, 2 and 4 are untouched by this batch, so they receive zero gradient in the backward pass.

blocks.md: Because an embedding is just a weight matrix, backpropagation trains it like any other layer: the gradient of the loss with respect to a looked-up row is the gradient flowing into that row's output, and rows that were not looked up get exactly zero. That sparsity is why PyTorch offers `sparse=True`, which returns a sparse gradient; its docs note that only some optimizers support it (`optim.SGD`, `optim.SparseAdam`, and `optim.Adagrad` on CPU).

The memory cost is $W \times d$ numbers. A 50,000-word vocabulary with $d = 300$ is 15,000,000 parameters, so embedding tables are often the largest single layer in models that handle large vocabularies or catalogs of IDs.

An embedding is a learned weight matrix indexed by item ID. Meaning is not built in: the vectors start random and become useful only because some training objective rewards putting related items close together. The rest of this course is about which objectives do that.

blocks.question: A batch contains the token IDs [2, 2, 4] and the model uses an embedding table with 5 rows. After one backward pass, which rows of the table have a nonzero gradient?
options: All 5 rows, because the whole matrix is a parameter
Rows 2 and 4, with row 2's gradient being the sum of two contributions
Rows 2 and 4, with row 2's gradient counted once because duplicates are removed
Only row 4, because repeated tokens cancel out
blocks.explain: Only looked-up rows get gradient, and a row looked up twice accumulates both contributions (the lookup's backward pass is a scatter-add). Rows 0, 1 and 3 get exactly zero, which is what makes sparse updates possible.

blocks.question: Why do the dense vectors let a model generalize from cat to kitten when one-hot codes do not?
options: Dense vectors have more dimensions, so they hold more information
The dot product of two one-hot vectors is undefined
Nearby inputs produce nearby activations, so what the network learned for one word partly applies to the other
Dense vectors are normalized to length 1
blocks.explain: The downstream layers are smooth functions of their input. If kitten's vector is close to cat's, the network's output for kitten is close to its output for cat. One-hot codes have more dimensions, not fewer, and their dot products are well defined (just always 0).

lessons.title: Learning word vectors by predicting their neighbours

blocks.md: Where does a training signal for *cat is like kitten* come from without labels? The **distributional hypothesis** (Harris, 1954) says that words occurring in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings. *Cat* and *kitten* both show up near *purr*, *fed*, *the*, *litter*. If we train vectors to predict a word's neighbours, words with similar neighbours are pushed toward similar vectors.

**Skip-gram**, from Mikolov et al. (2013) and released as the word2vec tool, turns that into a prediction task. Slide over text. At each position the word there is the *center* word, and every word within $c$ positions on either side is a *context* word. Each (center, context) pair is a training example: given the center, predict the context.

blocks.title: Skip-gram pairs from one sentence, window c = 2

scenes.caption: Center the (position 0). Context: cat, sat. 2 pairs so far.
Center cat. Context: the, sat, on. Running total 5 pairs.
Center sat: a full window of 4 context words. Running total 9 pairs.
Center on: context cat, sat, the, mat. Running total 13 pairs.
Center the again (position 4). Its pairs are added to the same word's statistics. Running total 16 pairs.
Center mat: context on, the. Total 18 pairs from a 6-word sentence. word2vec streams billions of these.

blocks.md: Each word gets **two** vectors: an *input* vector $v_w$, used when the word is the center, and an *output* vector $u_w$, used when it is a context. Both are rows of embedding matrices of shape $W \times d$. The original skip-gram scores a context word $o$ for center $c$ with a softmax over the whole vocabulary:

blocks.caption: Skip-gram softmax (Mikolov et al., 2013b, eq. 2, with v as input and u as output vectors). Training maximizes the average log of this over all pairs.

blocks.prompt: For one training pair, how many dot products does the softmax denominator need if the vocabulary has 1,000,000 words?
blocks.reveal: **All 1,000,000**, one per vocabulary word, and the gradient touches every output vector. Mikolov et al. note that the cost of the gradient of $\log p(w_O \mid w_I)$ is proportional to $W$, which is often $10^5$ to $10^7$. With billions of pairs this is far too slow, which is the problem the next lesson's negative sampling solves.

blocks.title: Skip-gram: full softmax vs negative sampling

scenes.caption: The center word's ID selects its input vector v_cat. Output vectors u_w live in a second table.
Full softmax: every one of the W output vectors is dotted with v_cat and normalized. Cost per pair grows with the vocabulary size.
Negative sampling (next lesson): only the true context and k sampled noise words are scored, each with an independent sigmoid. With k = 5 that is 6 dot products instead of W.

blocks.md: Skip-gram is not trained to be a good language model; the prediction task is a pretext. Mikolov et al. say plainly that the skip-gram model is only concerned with learning high-quality vector representations. After training, the output layer is usually thrown away and the input vectors are kept as the embeddings.

A sibling architecture, **CBOW** (continuous bag of words, from the same 2013 paper), flips the direction: it averages the context vectors and predicts the center word. Both rely on the same idea: the only supervision is the text itself, so any large corpus becomes training data. This is the first example of **self-supervised** representation learning in this course.

blocks.question: With window $c = 2$, how many (center, context) pairs does the 6-word sentence *the cat sat on the mat* produce?
blocks.explain: Edge words have fewer neighbours: positions 0 and 5 get 2 context words each, positions 1 and 4 get 3, positions 2 and 3 get 4. That is 2 + 3 + 4 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 18. The naive 6 x 4 = 24 forgets that the window is cut off at the sentence edges.

blocks.question: Two words, *Paris* and *Rome*, never appear in the same sentence in the training corpus. Can skip-gram still give them similar vectors?
options: No, they must co-occur to be pulled together
Yes, if they share many context words such as city, capital and visited
Only if they are in the same window at least once
Only with CBOW, not skip-gram
blocks.explain: Similarity comes from shared contexts, not direct co-occurrence. Both input vectors are trained to score highly against the same output vectors (u_city, u_capital, ...), which pushes them toward the same region of the space.

lessons.title: Negative sampling: one word2vec update by hand

blocks.md: Negative sampling replaces the $W$-way softmax with a much cheaper question: *is this (center, context) pair real, or noise?* For each real pair, draw $k$ **negative** words from a noise distribution $P_n$ and train a logistic classifier to say yes to the real pair and no to each negative. Mikolov et al. (2013b) define the objective for one pair, to be maximized, as:

blocks.caption: Skip-gram with negative sampling (SGNS). Here sigma(x) = 1/(1+exp(-x)) and sigma(-x) = 1 - sigma(x). In training the expectation is replaced by k samples.

blocks.md: This is just the binary cross-entropy you know from logistic regression, applied to dot products. Its gradients are short. With $s_o = \sigma(u_o^\top v_c)$ and $s_i = \sigma(u_{w_i}^\top v_c)$, the loss $L$ (the negative of the objective) has $\partial L/\partial u_o = (s_o - 1)\, v_c$, $\partial L/\partial u_{w_i} = s_i\, v_c$, and $\partial L/\partial v_c = (s_o - 1)\, u_o + \sum_i s_i\, u_{w_i}$.

Read the signs: the real context vector moves *toward* $v_c$, each negative moves *away*, and $v_c$ moves toward $u_o$ and away from the negatives. Let us do one step by hand with $d = 2$, center *cat*, real context *sat*, one negative *car* ($k = 1$), and learning rate 0.5. The starting vectors are small, as after random initialization.

blocks.title: One SGNS update for the pair (cat, sat)
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
sig = lambda x: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))
v = np.array([0.2, 0.1])       # input vector of cat
u_pos = np.array([0.3, -0.1])  # output vector of sat (real context)
u_neg = np.array([0.4, 0.3])   # output vector of car (noise sample)
lr = 0.5

s_pos = sig(u_pos @ v)   # model's P(real) for (cat, sat)
s_neg = sig(u_neg @ v)   # model's P(real) for (cat, car)
loss = -np.log(s_pos) - np.log(1 - s_neg)

g_v = (s_pos - 1) * u_pos + s_neg * u_neg
g_pos = (s_pos - 1) * v
g_neg = s_neg * v

v, u_pos, u_neg = v - lr * g_v, u_pos - lr * g_pos, u_neg - lr * g_neg
print(sig(u_pos @ v), sig(u_neg @ v))

scenes.caption: Start: three 2-d vectors. Only these three rows of the two tables take part in this step; the other W - 3 rows are untouched.
Scores: u_pos . v = 0.05 and u_neg . v = 0.11. Both sigmoids are near 0.5: the untrained model cannot tell the real pair from noise.
Loss = -ln(0.512) - ln(1 - 0.527) = 1.418. Two coin flips cost 2 ln 2 = 1.386, so we start slightly worse than chance.
Gradients. g_pos is negative (u_pos should move along +v), g_neg is positive (u_neg should move along -v).
SGD step: subtract lr times each gradient. Every update used the old values, computed before the assignment.
Re-score: P(real) for (cat, sat) rose to 0.515 and for (cat, car) fell to 0.514. Loss is now 1.386. Small steps, right direction.

blocks.title: Repeating the same update on this one pair

scenes.caption: Step 5: 0.556 vs 0.471, loss 1.224. Progress is slow while the vectors are tiny, because each gradient is scaled by the other vectors' small entries.
Step 10: 0.846 vs 0.177, loss 0.361. Once the vectors grow, each step makes a bigger difference.
Step 20: 0.981 vs 0.021, loss 0.041. Simplified: real training interleaves billions of different pairs with fresh negatives, so no single pair is fit this hard.

blocks.md: **Which negatives?** Mikolov et al. tried several noise distributions and found that the unigram distribution raised to the 3/4 power, $P_n(w) = U(w)^{3/4}/Z$, significantly outperformed both the plain unigram and the uniform distribution. Raising to 3/4 flattens the distribution: very frequent words are sampled a bit less and rare words a bit more. For $k$ they report 5 to 20 as useful for small datasets and as few as 2 to 5 for large ones.

blocks.title: Noise distribution for a toy corpus of 1,080 tokens

scenes.caption: Plain unigram: the would be 0.926 of all negatives, so most negative samples would teach almost nothing new.
Unigram to the 3/4: the drops to 0.84 while mat rises from 0.009 to 0.027, about 3x more often. Rarer words get more negative updates.

blocks.md: **Subsampling frequent words.** Words like *the* appear in almost every window and carry little information. The paper discards each occurrence of word $w$ during training with probability $P(w) = 1 - \sqrt{t / f(w)}$, where $f(w)$ is the word's frequency and $t$ is a threshold, typically around $10^{-5}$. They report it speeds up training and improves the vectors of rare words.

blocks.title: Subsampling: probability of discarding a word

scenes.caption: t = 1e-5. A word making up 5% of tokens is dropped 98.6% of the time; a word at 0.01% is dropped 68.4%. Words at or below t are always kept.
Raise t to 1e-4: the curve shifts right, so fewer words are subsampled and each is dropped less often.

blocks.md: The formula above is the one in the paper. The released word2vec C code uses a slightly different expression with a `sample` parameter, so if you are reproducing exact numbers, read the code of the implementation you use.

blocks.question: Mid-training, a negative sample $w_i$ already has $\sigma(u_{w_i}^\top v_c) = 0.01$. How much does this negative change $u_{w_i}$ in this step?
options: A lot, because negatives always get the full learning rate
Nothing, because negatives only update $v_c$
Very little, because its gradient is $0.01\, v_c$
It moves toward $v_c$, increasing the score
blocks.explain: The gradient for a negative is $s_i v_c$. When the model already gives it a tiny probability of being real, $s_i$ is near 0 and so is the update. Easy negatives teach little, which is one reason the choice of noise distribution matters.

blocks.question: Why is SGNS so much cheaper per training pair than the full softmax?
options: It uses smaller vectors
It skips the input vector update
It only trains on frequent words
It touches $k + 1$ output vectors instead of all $W$
blocks.explain: The softmax normalizer needs every output vector; the negative sampling objective needs only the true context and the k samples. With k = 5 and W = 1,000,000 that is 6 dot products instead of a million.

lessons.title: What the geometry means: cosine, analogies and PMI

blocks.md: Trained vectors are compared with **cosine similarity**, $\cos(a, b) = a^\top b / (\lVert a \rVert \lVert b \rVert)$, the dot product of the two vectors after scaling each to length 1. Cosine ignores vector length and looks only at direction. Nearest neighbours under cosine are how you look up similar words, products or documents.

Mikolov et al. (2013a) found that relationships appear as roughly consistent **offsets**. To answer *man is to king as woman is to ?*, compute $x = v_{king} - v_{man} + v_{woman}$ and return the vocabulary word whose vector is closest to $x$ by cosine. The paper adds a detail that is easy to miss: *we discard the input question words during this search*.

blocks.prompt: Why would excluding the three input words matter? Guess before looking at the toy example below.
blocks.reveal: Because $x$ is usually still closest to **king** itself. Subtracting *man* and adding *woman* changes only a small gender component; everything else that makes *king* distinctive stays. Nissim et al. (2020) re-ran the standard analogy test on the GoogleNews vectors: accuracy (micro) was 0.74 with input words excluded and 0.21 when they were allowed, mostly because the answer came back as the second word (*king*).

blocks.title: Cosine to king - man + woman (toy 6-d vectors)

scenes.caption: Toy vectors built so the gender difference is small, as in real data. Unconstrained nearest neighbour: king (0.934) beats queen (0.766).
Exclude the input words man, king and woman, as the paper does. Now queen (0.766) wins over prince (0.672). The famous result depends on this rule.

blocks.md: Vector arithmetic analogies are a nice demo, not a law. The answer depends on excluding inputs, and Nissim et al. show that other implementation choices (casing, frequency cutoffs, the exact formula) change results too. The same arithmetic surfaces social biases: Bolukbasi et al. (2016) found that the GoogleNews word2vec vectors complete *man : computer programmer :: woman : x* with *homemaker*.

**What is SGNS actually computing?** Levy and Goldberg (2014) showed that, if $d$ is large enough for each dot product to take any value, the SGNS objective is maximized when $v_w^\top u_c = \mathrm{PMI}(w, c) - \log k$, where pointwise mutual information compares how often $w$ and $c$ co-occur with how often they would by chance (their analysis uses the empirical unigram as the noise distribution). So SGNS implicitly factorizes a **shifted PMI matrix** of word-context counts.

blocks.caption: #(w, c): pairs with center w and context c. |D|: total pairs. #(w), #(c): how often w is a center and c a context.

blocks.title: Pair counts #(w, c) for the 18 pairs of lesson 2

scenes.caption: Rows are center words, columns context words. Each count is a pair from the sliding window; the total over all cells is 18.
(sat, the) occurs 2 times. sat is a center 4 times and the is a context 5 times, so PMI = ln(2 x 18 / (4 x 5)) = ln 1.8 = 0.588: they co-occur 1.8x more than chance.
With k = 5, SGNS's optimum for this cell is 0.588 - ln 5 = -1.022. Cells with count 0, like (cat, mat), have PMI of minus infinity; SGNS never reaches that, it just pushes the dot product low.

blocks.md: This links prediction-based embeddings to older count-based methods. **GloVe** (Pennington et al., 2014) fits it directly: it minimizes a weighted least-squares loss so that $w_i^\top \tilde w_j + b_i + \tilde b_j \approx \log X_{ij}$, where $X_{ij}$ counts co-occurrences, with weight $f(x) = (x/x_{max})^{\alpha}$ below $x_{max} = 100$ and 1 above, and $\alpha = 3/4$. Both families turn co-occurrence statistics into low-dimensional vectors.

Static word embeddings encode co-occurrence statistics. Similar vectors mean *used in similar contexts*, which often but not always means *similar meaning*: antonyms like hot and cold share many contexts too.

blocks.question: Your search for words similar to *cheap* returns *expensive* near the top. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Antonyms share most of their contexts (prices, tickets, very), so distributional training places them close
A bug: cosine similarity must be negative for antonyms
The vectors were not normalized before training
Negative sampling inverts antonym vectors
blocks.explain: The objective only sees contexts. *Cheap* and *expensive* appear around the same words, so their vectors align. Nothing in SGNS or GloVe pushes antonyms to negative cosine.

blocks.question: A teammate reports that *king - man + woman* returns *king* in your system. What is the best first check?
options: Retrain with a larger dimension
Switch from cosine to Euclidean distance
Whether the nearest-neighbour search excludes the three query words, as the original evaluation did
Increase the number of negative samples
blocks.explain: Returning an input word is the expected behaviour when inputs are not excluded: Nissim et al. measured 0.21 accuracy unconstrained vs 0.74 constrained on the same vectors.

lessons.title: Beyond words: contrastive learning and failure modes

blocks.md: Word vectors are one case of a general idea. Bengio, Courville and Vincent (2013) frame **representation learning** as learning transformations of the data that make it easier to extract useful information for later predictors, instead of hand-engineering features. In a trained network every hidden layer is such a representation; an embedding is simply the representation of a discrete ID.

Three common ways to get a useful representation:

- **Supervised**: train on a labelled task and reuse a late hidden layer (for example the layer before an image classifier's output).
- **Reconstruction**: an *autoencoder* compresses the input to a small code and decodes it back; the code is the representation.
- **Contrastive**: pull together representations of two views of the same thing and push apart views of different things. Skip-gram with negative sampling already does this for (word, context) pairs.

The contrastive recipe generalizes SGNS from one negative at a time to a softmax over a set. **InfoNCE** (van den Oord et al., 2018) scores one positive among $N$ candidates ($N - 1$ negatives) with a categorical cross-entropy. **SimCLR** (Chen et al., 2020) uses it for images as the *NT-Xent* loss: two random augmentations of each image are positives, the other $2(N-1)$ augmented images in the batch are negatives, and similarity is cosine divided by a **temperature** $\tau$.

blocks.caption: NT-Xent for a positive pair (i, j), as in SimCLR. sim is cosine similarity; the sum runs over the other 2N - 1 examples in the batch.

blocks.md: Worked example: an anchor has cosine 0.9 with its positive and 0.6, 0.3 and -0.2 with three negatives ($N = 4$ candidates). Uniform guessing would give loss $\ln 4 = 1.386$. The temperature decides how sharply the softmax separates these similarities.

blocks.title: Softmax over 4 candidates at different temperatures

scenes.caption: tau = 1: probabilities [0.381, 0.282, 0.209, 0.127]. The positive gets only 0.381 and the loss is 0.964, even though it has the highest cosine.
tau = 0.5: positive 0.51, loss 0.673. Dividing by a smaller tau stretches the gaps between similarities.
tau = 0.1: positive 0.95, loss 0.051. Among the negatives, almost all the push now goes to the hardest one (0.6, weight 0.047); the easy ones (0.002 and 0.000) get about nothing.

blocks.title: Probability of the positive vs temperature

scenes.caption: Positive at 0.9: lowering tau drives its probability toward 1 because it is the most similar candidate.

Positive at 0.5, below the hardest negative (0.6): lowering tau now drives its probability toward 0, so the loss and its gradient grow large. (The dots still mark the 0.9 case.) Low tau focuses training on hard cases.

blocks.md: SimCLR reports that both $\ell_2$ normalization and a properly tuned temperature matter a lot, and that in their CIFAR-10 sweep the best of $\{0.1, 0.5, 1.0\}$ at convergence was 0.5. InfoNCE also has a useful reading: van den Oord et al. show that $\log N - L_N$ is a lower bound on the mutual information (how many nats knowing one view tells you about the other) between the two views, which tightens as $N$ grows. That is one reason contrastive methods like large batches.

blocks.title: SimCLR: where the representation is taken

scenes.caption: Two random augmentations of the same image form the positive pair; the same encoder f processes both.
The loss is computed on z = g(h), the output of a small projection head.
But the representation kept for downstream tasks is h, before the head. SimCLR found h better than z by more than 10% in linear evaluation: the head absorbs information the loss throws away.

blocks.md:
**Failure modes and fixes in practice:**

- **Unknown words.** A word-level table has no row for a word unseen in training. fastText (Bojanowski et al., 2017) represents a word as the sum of vectors for its character n-grams (n from 3 to 6, plus the whole word), so new words get a vector from their pieces.
- **One vector per word.** *Bank* gets a single vector mixing river and money senses. Contextual embeddings from Transformers, the next course, fix this by computing a vector per occurrence.
- **Bias.** Vectors reflect their corpus, including stereotypes, as the analogy example showed.

Embeddings come from an objective, not from the lookup table. Pick the objective so that items you want close (words in the same contexts, two views of one image, a user and the items they clicked) are pushed together and everything else is pushed apart.

blocks.question: You train a contrastive image model with $\tau = 1$ and unnormalized dot products. The contrastive loss falls nicely, but a linear classifier trained on the representation scores poorly. Which change does SimCLR's ablation most directly support?
options: Remove the negatives so the model only sees positives
Increase tau to 10 to smooth the loss
Take the representation from z instead of h
Use cosine similarity (l2 normalization) with a tuned, smaller temperature
blocks.explain: SimCLR reports that without l2 normalization the contrastive task gets easier but the representation is worse under linear evaluation, and that a proper temperature matters too. Removing negatives invites collapse (everything maps to one point), a larger tau flattens the softmax further, and h, not z, is the better representation.

blocks.question: Your product catalog adds thousands of new item IDs every day, and the model uses one learned embedding row per ID. What problem should you expect for brand-new items?
options: Their rows are still at their random initialization because they have received no gradient, so their similarities are meaningless
None, embeddings generalize to any ID
They will all collapse to the zero vector
Their vectors will equal the average of all rows
blocks.explain: A row learns only when its ID appears in training. New IDs keep their random initial vectors (in PyTorch drawn from N(0, 1)). Systems handle this cold-start problem by building vectors from content features, the same idea fastText uses with character n-grams.
